one_liner: Cranelift, Wasmtime's Rust code generator: in a 2021 paper it compiled WebAssembly 7-10x faster than LLVM-based WAVM, with code about 14% slower.
what_it_does: Cranelift is a retargetable code generator that lowers its own SSA intermediate representation (Cranelift IR) to x86-64, aarch64, s390x or riscv64 machine code. You use it as Rust crates: cranelift-frontend builds IR, cranelift-codegen compiles it, and cranelift-jit or cranelift-object emits into memory or an object file. Wasmtime embeds it as the optimizing tier of a standalone WebAssembly runtime, and C and C++ hosts reach it only through Wasmtime's C API (wasm.h, wasi.h, wasmtime.h, CMake build) or the C++ wasmtime.hh header, not through a Cranelift C API. It is not a drop-in replacement for V8 or LLVM: you either emit Cranelift IR from Rust or hand Wasmtime a Wasm module.
how_it_is_fast: A single IR runs from the frontend through register allocation, instead of LLVM's chain of LLVM IR, SelectionDAG, MachineInstr and MC layers (docs/compare-llvm.md). Mid-end rewrites run on an e-graph built inside the data-flow graph (codegen/src/egraph), with optional alias analysis that removes redundant loads; instruction selection is written as ISLE rewrite rules (prelude_lower.isle and per-ISA rules). Registers come from regalloc2, either a backtracking allocator with live-range splitting or a single_pass allocator that compiles faster but spills more, and the codegen crates avoid call-stack recursion.
when_to_use: Embedding a WebAssembly sandbox in a C, C++ or Rust service where compile latency for each module matters and an LLVM-based ahead-of-time engine is about 10x slower to compile (paper Fig. 18: about 100-110x copy-and-patch startup delay for Wasmtime Cranelift against about 800-1100x for WAVM).
Writing a JIT or debug-build backend in Rust that should compile much faster than LLVM while keeping code in the range of an optimizing tier (the same codegen drives rustc_codegen_cranelift).

Multi-tenant hosts that need a maintained security process: fuzzing against V8 and the executable Wasm spec, a regalloc2 checker, published advisories and patched LTS branches (for example 36.0.17 on 2026-10-02).
Targets limited to x86-64 (System V and Windows x64), aarch64 (Linux and macOS) on Apple silicon, s390x or riscv64; SIMD is complete on x86-64 and aarch64.
when_not_to_use: Peak throughput with compile time unimportant: LLVM via WAVM ran the PolyBenchC average about 14% faster and CoreMark in about 0.43 s against 0.59 s.

As an alternative to V8 TurboFan on both axes: in the same paper TurboFan compiled faster on CoreMark, PolyBenchC and clang.wasm, tied on AutoCAD, and its PolyBenchC code was about 2% faster (Cranelift was faster only on CoreMark, 0.59 s against 0.94 s).

Startup-dominated workloads of small or huge modules: baseline compilers start far sooner (copy-and-patch had two to three orders of magnitude lower startup delay than the optimizing compilers); inside Wasmtime that role belongs to the Winch baseline compiler, which had two Critical or Moderate sandbox advisories in April 2026.
C++-only toolchains that want to drive the code generator directly: Cranelift is Rust with no stable C API, and its README says its APIs are not yet considered stable.
Hosts outside the four backends (for example 32-bit x86 or 32-bit Arm); the README lists only x86-64, aarch64, s390x and riscv64.

integration.form: crate (cranelift-codegen, cranelift-frontend, cranelift-jit, cranelift-object); for C and C++ hosts, the Wasmtime C API library with wasm.h, wasi.h, wasmtime.h and the C++ wasmtime.hh header
integration.dependencies: cranelift-codegen: regalloc2, hashbrown, smallvec, bumpalo, target-lexicon, log, rustc-hash, libm and sibling cranelift-* crates (gimli, capstone, serde optional); Wasmtime adds many more
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.97.0 on main and for 0.137.0-rc.1 (policy: at most current stable minus 2), Rust 1.96.0 for cranelift-codegen 0.136.x; edition 2024
integration.platforms: x86-64 (System V and Windows x64 ABIs), aarch64 (Linux and macOS), s390x, riscv64
integration.thread_safety: not documented in the pages read

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the README numbers: '~2% slower than V8' and '~14% slower than WAVM' are ratios of Fig. 22 bars, each an arithmetic mean over 30 PolyBenchC kernels of times normalized to a third compiler (copy-and-patch), from only three runs with no confidence intervals. They are not a direct Cranelift-versus-TurboFan comparison, and Fig. 21 shows wide per-kernel scatter.

The numbers describe Wasmtime 0.26 in 2021 and depend on the embedding: the same Cranelift inside Wasmer 1.0 took about 1.12 s on CoreMark against 0.59 s under Wasmtime (Fig. 20), and current cranelift-codegen is 0.136.2 stable or 0.137.0-rc.1.

Raw Cranelift defaults are tuned for safety, not speed: opt_level defaults to none (the first enum value) and enable_verifier defaults to true, which the settings docs say makes compilation slower. Direct cranelift-jit users must set both before comparing compile or run time.

Sandbox safety rests on codegen correctness: CVE-2026-34971 (GHSA-jhxm-h53p-jm7w, CVSS 9.0) was an aarch64 miscompile of load(iadd(base, ishl(index, amt))) that allowed sandbox escape with 64-bit memories when Spectre mitigations or signals-based traps were off (fixed in 36.0.7, 42.0.2 and 43.0.1), and x86-64 f64.copysign and f64x2.splat produced out-of-sandbox loads (January and April 2026). Parts of the docs are stale: compare-llvm.md still says Cranelift does no mid-level optimization, and the README badge says rustc 1.37.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Cranelift over WasmNow or other copy-and-patch baseline compilers when code quality matters (copy-and-patch's PolyBenchC code was about 1.4x slower than Cranelift's in the same paper) and you need a maintained, security-supported production runtime. Pick TPDE instead when you already emit LLVM IR and only need faster -O0-class code generation, and V8 when you are inside a browser or Node.
verified_claims_summary: Xu and Kjolstad's OOPSLA 2021 paper (Intel i7-7700HQ at 2.8 GHz with turbo, Ubuntu 20.04, compilation pinned to one CPU) measured Wasmtime 0.26 Cranelift against Chrome 81 V8 TurboFan, Wasmer 1.0 and WAVM. Cranelift's startup delay was about 7-10x lower than WAVM's on CoreMark, PolyBenchC and clang.wasm, but its code was slower than WAVM's (PolyBenchC average about 0.70 against 0.61-0.62, CoreMark about 0.59 s against 0.43 s). Against TurboFan it was roughly even on code speed (0.70 against 0.69 on PolyBenchC; faster on CoreMark) and slower to compile on three of four modules. Wasm build flags and the harness are not public.
status_note: Very active: monthly Wasmtime majors (49.0.2 stable, 50.0.0-rc.1 on 2026-10-05), patched LTS branches and frequent security releases, Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception, about 51.6M crates.io downloads for cranelift-codegen; the only third-party numbers measured Wasmtime 0.26 five years ago.
